meta.title: Compass — Visibility 2x2 working set

x.label: can a normal user get this quickly today?

meta.note: Every score here is a blind panel consensus, not the author's estimate. Three independent lenses scored all 57 items without seeing the original numbers or notes, 171 scores in total, and the median of the three is the value shown. Two overrides applied on top: an item that is an ACTION has its access read as how hard it is to DO today, and a strong adversarial finding beats the panel. Impact carries a separate detector-risk discount wherever the feature only works if a heuristic is right. 10 items are strict subsets of another and are hidden by 'primaries only'. A further 9 are narrower than something else and score HIGHER than it, so they are kept: a cheaper route that outranks its own superset is the version to build, not the version to hide.

archetypes.name: Don't burn capacity
archetypes.blurb: The agent stops because the quota ran out, not because the work finished.

archetypes.name: Don't be the bottleneck
archetypes.blurb: The agent is waiting on you and you don't know it.

archetypes.name: Steer before waste
archetypes.blurb: It is going the wrong way and will keep going until someone looks.

archetypes.name: Spend attention well
archetypes.blurb: Knowing you are free matters as much as knowing you are needed.

archetypes.name: Nothing dies quietly
archetypes.blurb: Finished, crashed, and abandoned all look the same from outside.

archetypes.name: Move up a level
archetypes.blurb: Change what the user's job is, not how well they watch.

columns.name: Open Session(s)
columns.question: Which of my agents are running?
columns.promise: Every session on this machine, across ten harnesses, on one screen, with what is active now kept apart from what is only recent history.

columns.name: Mid-flight
columns.question: What is it doing, and when should I come back?
columns.promise: For each live session, what it is doing now, what it plans next, how far into the current turn it is, and an estimate of when that turn ends. It tells you when that changes instead of making you poll. The first screen sets your goal or a permitted prompt beside current activity and brings recorded departures forward. The session page tells you once what a reading sends and where, without steering it for you. Pause model calls stops Analyze drift, goal summaries and session summaries until Resume model calls. Turn off summaries stops session summaries only; while paused it stays disabled and keeps its saved answer. Open a session, set a goal and press Analyze drift. The How Intent and drift works entry in the Intent card's More menu explains the steps and the limits; with no outcome line, Compass reads your goal's end state; a goal too vague to read is refused under the Goal field, with no level for that run. On Claude Code sessions, you can turn on a live drift estimate in the panel and header after every turn, based on recorded checks and file paths rather than the meaning of your intent. An analysis shows its level, each outcome line against the recorded work and what the agent said with its source, where files were written, and why a result is stale. Recorded checks and file paths include subagent work, labelled as such. On Claude Code sessions, What the session has done tells the session as a short story in phases, each line citing the entries it rests on, written by a model through your own Claude Code. A finished session is summarized when you open it and a running one when you press Summarize or Update summary; the first summary says what is sent and where, with Turn off summaries beside it. A summary does not say in its own voice that the work is done, and a citation shows where a line came from, not that the line is right. Reader-requested readings are capped at 100 attempts per rolling twenty-four hours. With no saved goal, a check adopts the goal drafted from your first Claude Code or Codex prompt (your latest where no first one with a time is published); the goal field also offers your latest prompt. Adopted words are marked, and missing source times refuse adoption. Claude Code and Codex hooks also report matched destructive command shapes; a match does not prove success. Compass saves a stage you choose for a Spacedock workflow and alerts once when it observes an entity enter that stage; gaps and unavailable sources are stated, and a notification request does not prove a banner appeared.

columns.name: Stopped at Gate
columns.question: Is anything waiting on me?
columns.promise: One queue of everything blocked on you, with what it is waiting for and how long it has waited. A session can also ask you a question directly and wait for your answer.

columns.name: Usage
columns.question: Will I hit the wall before the work finishes?
columns.promise: Your quota in one place across vendors, with each window's budget shown against its own clock, so you can see whether there is room before you start rather than partway through.

columns.name: End of sessions
columns.question: Did anything die quietly?
columns.promise: Nothing finishes invisibly. Work that finished and was never read is flagged, and a session that ends leaving uncommitted changes says so.

states.name: Partly there
states.hint: Data exists; the decision does not

states.name: Not yet
states.hint: Needs a new source or a new power

reviewNotes: All 57 items were re-scored by three blind lenses across two rounds, 171 independent scores. The author's originals are gone by request; what remains is the vetted consensus.

The audit found the author's bias was on the WRONG AXIS from what anyone suspected. Access inflation was small: +4.4 inside the differentiated quadrant against -3.1 outside. Impact inflation was large and consistent at +10.3, repeating at +6.6 in the second round even after the rubric was corrected. Of the ten items that fell out of the quadrant, eight fell on impact alone and none on access alone. The author was not pushing items sideways into the corner; they were overstating how much anyone would DO with the information.

Two mechanical biases were verified against the raw data rather than taken on trust. The axis realignment was a one-way ratchet: 43 of 57 items moved up by an average of +38.1 points and only 13 moved down, which is a new prior wearing a new definition's clothes. And flagged favourites carried a measurable premium, averaging impact 73.5 against 61.0 for unflagged items, concentrated on impact because that is the axis with no external check.

The largest structural finding is redundancy. Twenty-one strict subset relationships were found across the board: C5 within C2, B3 and B5 within B4, D6 within D5, A1 and A2 and A5 within A9, E1 within E2 and E3, F1 within F6. The board reads as 57 features and is nearer 47 once duplicates fold in. Redundancy penalties are held as metadata rather than subtracted from impact, because they only bite once the primary ships. Nine of those subsets score HIGHER than the item containing them, including E4 over E5 and C5 over C2, which inverts the usual reading: the narrow slice is the thing to build and the broad version is the thing to defer. [Dated: this census is the audit's finding, and decisions have moved under it. A9 was cut on 2026-08-06, so the five relations recorded within it — A1, A2, A5, A6 and G1 — describe an item that will not be built; their redundantWith blocks are gone from the items, and A1 and A2 have since shipped. No score moved either way, because the penalties were always metadata. The live field is subsetOf, which is what 'primaries only' filters on and which ten items still carry; audit/g2-redundancy.jsonl holds the census itself, and each item's own verdict and decisionNote hold what has happened since.]

Detector risk is now priced separately. Ten items score high on access precisely because no tool anywhere computes the number, which is not access being withheld but a number that does not exist. Their value rests on a heuristic being accurate. C2 takes the largest discount among the strong items at -30, which is the honest cost of the fact that a false all-clear sends someone away from a wedged agent.

Two action items were badly misread as information. D7 was scored 72 for access when it is a sort order that already ships behind a toggle, so its do-access is 12. E7 was scored 62 when it is a sentence the user types, so its do-access is 15. Both corrections are large enough to move them off the board's high-value list.

D1, the disputed placement, is settled and the board was closer than the author. Consensus access is 52 against the author's 65, because tmux list-panes and capture-pane let a competent developer sweep every session in one pass. The author's own principle was too broad: the fleet is a loop, and only correlation over TIME is genuinely beyond reach. Impact came in at 65, above the author's 52, so the error ran in both directions.

E4, ended with uncommitted work, was promoted on a strong twice-confirmed finding. It is the one place the pane sweep has no answer, because an ended session has no pane and no process. That is the general test for future items: does answering it require a session that no longer exists?

The impact>=70 line is fragile and should not be presented as a hard binary. Twenty items sit between 63 and 75 on impact (twelve of them on the high-access side where the line alone decides the quadrant), and a five-point move in the threshold roughly doubles the quadrant count. The band is drawn on the map for that reason.

How to read these notes: they are the audit's own record, written when it ran, and they are not rewritten as the board moves. Counts and item lists in them describe the board of that date. Where a later decision contradicts one, the item carries the current state in its verdict, decisionNote and subsetNote fields, and the note here is only how the board got there.

items.signal: 5h window % used, and when it resets
items.note: From the workshop board, and the most-cited pain on it: force-paused mid-job, restart by hand after the reset. Under the realigned axis it is the closest thing here to a commodity, at access 24, because /usage is one command away and a Barista-style status line puts it on screen unprompted. That is not an argument to cut it. It is the prerequisite for A2, A3, A4, A5, A7, A8, A9 and E7, so treat it as plumbing rather than a feature, and never ship it alone: on its own it spends a security amendment to save the user a glance at a status line. [Shipped since, so the sequencing advice above is a record of the argument rather than a live instruction.]
items.needs: Done. DEC-1 resolved on 2026-08-04 and the numbers now arrive three ways: the server fetches Claude's (and Cursor's) with the vendor's own token, Codex's are read from the rate-limit snapshots it already writes to disk, and Antigravity pushes its own in as a receipt. A vendor with no quota authority of its own still shows nothing.

items.signal: Weekly window % used, and when it resets
items.outcome: plan the week, not the hour
items.note: The 5h window governs the next job. The weekly window governs whether to start a big one at all on a Thursday.
items.needs: Done. The weekly window ships wherever the 5-hour one does, and a Codex plan that publishes only the weekly one publishes without it.

items.signal: Per-model sub-limits, Opus against Sonnet
items.note: More actionable than the aggregate, because the remedy is one keystroke rather than a two-hour wait. The board already records the user doing this by hand: hold off until the 5h limit resets, or switch to a different model.
items.needs: Same source as A1. The per-model fields sit alongside it.

items.signal: Capacity across subscriptions and harnesses
items.outcome: move the work to another harness
items.note: From the workshop board, with a worked example on it: Claude at 95%, Codex at 10%, migrate to Codex and keep going. I previously scored this 72 and called that placement wrong. The realigned axis says he was closer than I was. Every harness does show its own usage, so each piece is accessible to a user and it is the comparison that is tedious, which puts it mid-scale at 50 rather than hard [the author's re-score; the blind panel's median subsequently landed at 65, the value shown]. My 72 was measuring Compass's build cost, which is real but belongs in the build score, and it is still 70 there.
items.needs: A separate integration per vendor, each with its own auth. DEC-1 gets amended once, but this work repeats.

redundantWith.remains: Only the case where the whole account is capped, not just one model: every model at the ceiling, or a single-model harness. Then a fresh vendor is the only hatch left. Everything else about it is A1 replicated per vendor plus a comparison, at build 70 with per-vendor auth, and the user still pays to restate the task in another harness. Its own re-score to access 50 [panel median now 65] concedes each vendor already shows its own usage.

items.signal: Burn rate projected to the wall
items.outcome: decide now, not at the wall
items.note: 80% of 5h used is a number. Hitting the wall in 22 minutes is a decision. The realignment moves this from the convenience corner to the differentiated one, at access 72, because no status line projects a burn rate and nobody computes it by hand. It is the item that converts A1 from a readout into a reason to act, which is the strongest argument for paying DEC-1's cost at all.
items.needs: A1 supplies the ceiling. Everything else is already built.
items.inferred: Forward consumption rate, extrapolated from recent token or request throughput to a time-of-exhaustion. The series is non-stationary and bursty: an agent that just went idle carries a stale high rate, a compaction or a large file read spikes it, and the burn over the next hour depends mostly on what the user chooses to launch next, which is not in the data at all.

items.signal: Overrun likelihood before you start
items.outcome: don't start what you can't finish
items.note: From the board: work out the likelihood of overrun before starting the task. It needs a size estimate for work that has not begun, which is the part nobody does well.
items.needs: Shape-matching against similar past sessions, which needs H1. Speculative even then.
items.inferred: The size of work that has not started yet, matched by shape against similar past sessions (H1), then turned into a probability of overrunning the window. Two stacked guesses: that a prompt's text predicts its duration, and that a past session was 'similar'.
items.subsetNote: A6 subset of A9's question - both answer 'should I start', A6 adding a task-size estimate that needs H1 and stays speculative. [A9 is cut as of 2026-08-06, so this relation is historical. A6 is still hidden by 'primaries only' while the field stands.]

items.signal: Which session is eating the quota
items.outcome: kill that one, not all of them
items.note: Turns 'I am at 80%' into a target. Compass already attributes output tokens per session, so this is that number over the pool.
items.needs: A1 for the denominator. Per-session attribution already works.
items.inferred: That local output-token share equals share of the quota pool. It does not: quota consumption is weighted across input, cache and output, is per-model, is partly request-count based, and includes consumers Compass cannot see at all (Claude Desktop, web, another machine on the same account). The ranking is a proxy dressed as an attribution.
items.decisionNote: Closed as infeasible in favour of A10, 2026-08-06. The detector line above is the reason: local output-token share is not share of the quota pool, and no reweighting fixes the consumers Compass cannot see. A10 answers the same question from numbers Compass already has, which is what its preferredOver already recorded.

items.signal: Which session is burning fastest right now
items.outcome: pick the right one to stop
items.note: The version of A7 that needs no quota at all. Ranking sessions by output rate answers 'which one do I stop' without knowing the ceiling, and Compass already has every number involved. This is what lets Release 1 say something in the Usage column instead of leaving the board's biggest cluster blank until DEC-1 resolves.
items.needs: Nothing new. Sort the rate Compass already shows, and put it somewhere you can act on.

redundantWith.remains: Instantaneous rate catches a session that has just started burning hard, before cumulative share moves enough to rank it, and it needs no quota source at all so it can ship in Release 1 while DEC-1 is unresolved. Beyond that it answers the identical question with a weaker denominator; its own note calls it 'the version of A7 that needs no quota', which is a substitute, not an addition.

items.cheaperRoute: Narrower than A7 and scores higher, so it is the version to build.

items.signal: Cost per session
items.note: Low for a subscription user, because the cost is already sunk. It rises for API-key and team accounts, so this is a question about which segment we are building for rather than about value in the abstract. For the person on this board it stays low.
items.needs: Spend fields arrive in the same payload as A1.

items.signal: A single safe-to-start light
items.outcome: one glance before a long job
items.note: The usage cluster collapsed into one indicator. Users do not want a quota dashboard, they want permission to begin. Its information difficulty is exactly A1's, because it reads the same number. The extra cost is design, not data.
items.needs: Composes A1, A2 and A5. No source beyond A1.
items.inferred: A binary verdict, 'safe to start', composed from A5's projection plus a threshold nobody can set correctly because the tool does not know how large the job the user is about to start is. Collapsing to one bit also discards the nuance that would let the user sanity-check the call.
items.decisionNote: Killed by the owner, 2026-08-06. A9 was the redundancy primary for A1, A2, A5, A6 and G1, and those five penalties are lifted with it. No score moves: the penalties were held as metadata and never subtracted from impact, which is what the reviewNotes say and what audit/verify-scores.py computes.

items.signal: Session needs user input
items.note: A workshop card, and Compass's best signal. Shipped through transcript detection plus lifecycle hooks, with a native popup on macOS. Worth noticing that the board placed this right of centre rather than at the easy end. For Claude alone the information is easy, so that placement only makes sense if the room was already thinking across harnesses. If so, the dot was encoding B2 before anyone named it.
items.needs: Done, for Claude. B2 is the rest of it.

items.signal: Needs-input on the other eight harnesses
items.note: Compass's best signal works on one harness out of nine. Everything else about the product is presented as harness-agnostic, so users will assume this is too and will quietly miss gates on Codex and Copilot. One dot understates the spread: Copilot writes typed events and might expose it cheaply, while Pi has no passive needs-input signal at all. The 70 is an average across eight fairly different problems.
items.needs: Per-harness work. Hooks where a harness offers them, heuristics where it does not, and an honest blank where neither works.
items.inferred: Blocked-on-human state on eight harnesses that expose no such signal. Where typed events exist (Copilot) it is close to a read; where none exist (Pi, per the briefing) it is pattern matching on scrollback and session files across eight undocumented, independently version-drifting surfaces. The 'differentiated' score is an average over eight quite different detection problems.

items.signal: What it is waiting for, without opening it
items.note: The board asks for this twice: go back to the session for answering, and the file path that I need to review. For Claude the question text and its options already sit in the transcript record Compass reads to raise the flag. It parses them and then throws them away.
items.needs: Render what is already parsed. Cheapest real win in the gate column.

redundantWith.remains: As an independent capability, none: B4 cannot answer a prompt it has not rendered, so B3 is B4's first screen. Both are scored 78 for the same avoided trip. What survives is that B3 is shippable today with no DEC-2 write path, over data Compass already parses and throws away, and that reading the question is sometimes enough on its own (you learn it is asking to force-push and decide to go and look properly).

items.cheaperRoute: Narrower than B4 and scores higher, so it is the version to build.

items.signal: Answer it from Compass
items.outcome: the trip to the tab disappears
items.note: Marked down three times now, by three independent routes, which is usually the point to stop arguing. The adversarial pass said B5 captures much of the value far cheaper. The impact recalibration said ambition is not impact. The realigned axis now puts it at access 35, because going to the tab to answer a prompt is something a normal user can already do quickly. It saves keystrokes rather than creating access, so it is convenience with a very large build cost attached, which is the worst combination on the board.
items.needs: See DEC-2. It also cuts against the agnostic positioning, since a write path has to be built nine times.
items.scoreBasis: panel median of 3 blind lenses; boundary audit, demote, strong

items.signal: Click through to the session in the CLI
items.note: Already on the board. The cheap half of B4: it does not answer for you, it ends the hunt across tabs.
items.needs: Terminal focus is specific to the OS and the multiplexer. Solvable for tmux and iTerm, messy in general.

redundantWith.remains: Reaching sessions that are not at a gate: clicking into a working session to read its output, or into a stuck one C2 flagged. B4 only ever covers prompt-answering, so B5 keeps navigation for every other reason to visit a session. It is also the fallback when the write path does not exist for a given harness, which is most of them.

items.cheaperRoute: Narrower than B4 and scores higher, so it is the version to build.

items.signal: How long each has been blocked
items.note: Calm mode already shows wait time as the headline number on blocked rows.
items.needs: Done.
items.subsetNote: B6 subset of D7 - time-blocked is the attention sort's key, and B6 ships as exactly that headline number on blocked rows.

redundantWith.remains: The raw wait duration as evidence rather than as a sort key: '4 sessions blocked 40+ minutes today' is the number F3 needs to make the case for delegating. As triage it is fully absorbed, because time-blocked is precisely the key an attention sort already orders by, and it is shipped as exactly that headline number.

items.signal: Batch the gates into one queue
items.outcome: switch context once, not five times
items.note: Attention has a fixed cost per switch, so three separate pings cost more than one list of three. Answer top to bottom and clear the board. Note the gap between its two scores: the information is already on screen and all the cost is interface work. That is exactly the split the old single axis was hiding.
items.needs: B3, so each row says what it wants. No new data.
items.subsetNote: B7 subset of (D7 + B3) - a gate-filtered slice of the attention sort, with B3's text on each row; nothing in it is new information, and its note admits all the cost is interface.

redundantWith.remains: Net of the ordering, B7 is B3's per-row 'what it is waiting for' text plus an answer-top-to-bottom interaction. The genuine residue is the interaction: a single pass that clears N gates without leaving the surface, which a sorted list does not give you. Its own note concedes the information is already on screen and all the cost is interface, so what remains is a form, not a signal.

items.signal: Route a review request into a Spacedock gate
items.note: Board sticky: if the thing that needs input is a review, integrate with the gate. This is the seam where Compass stops being a separate tool and becomes part of Spacedock's flow.
items.needs: A Spacedock gate API, and a rule for deciding which prompts count as reviews.
items.inferred: Which prompts count as reviews. The item's own needs line admits it: 'a rule for deciding'. Without a model that is keyword matching on prompt text.

redundantWith.remains: The answer landing in Spacedock's own record so the first officer advances entity state, which a generic write into a terminal does not do. That is workflow bookkeeping rather than unblocking, and it is the seam where Compass joins Spacedock's flow instead of sitting beside it. Largely survives; the overlap is only the keystrokes.

items.signal: Subagent workflow stage, and a tripwire on it
items.note: From the workshop board. Half of it shipped, since the Spacedock stage strips show where each entity sits. The tripwire half, telling me when it crosses a line I set, does not exist. Information difficulty is moderate rather than high because Spacedock state files already say where everything is. What is missing is somewhere for the user to declare the line.
items.needs: A per-workflow condition, and a place to write it down.

redundantWith.remains: The user-declared threshold and a place to write it down, plus the alert edge. The stage strips are shipped and orthogonal. The tripwire half overlaps C3's comparison directly, and its delivery half is D4's; what is uniquely C1's is letting the user name the line rather than having the product infer it, which is also the thing that makes the signal trustworthy enough to leave on.

items.signal: Stuck, told apart from working
items.note: The board's own words make the case: from outside, a stuck agent looks exactly like a working agent, so you either sit and watch or you walk away and forget. There is no status line for this and no tab you can open to find out, which is what makes it differentiated rather than convenient. Everything Compass shows is derived from activity, and activity is what a wedged agent keeps producing, so the long-turn flag is a clock and not a diagnosis. The blind panel put it at impact 80 and access 78, and it was the only item an adversarial reviewer could not break. It then takes the largest detector-risk discount on the board at -30, which drops it to a risk-adjusted 50 and puts C5 above it: the loop detector needs a much narrower inference to be right, and that is the honest reason to build the narrow version first.
items.needs: New detection rather than new presentation: repeated identical tool calls, the same file rewritten over and over, a test re-run loop, recurring error strings. All of it already sits in transcripts Compass reads, which is why the information score is moderate while the build is not.
items.inferred: Intent. Whether an agent that is still emitting is productive or wedged, read off behavioural traces: repeated identical tool calls, the same file rewritten, a test re-run loop, recurring error strings. The problem is that those patterns are also what correct work looks like, and the genuinely novel wedges (an agent spiralling into longer plans, quietly redefining the task, waiting on a call that never returns) emit no repetition at all.

items.signal: Working outside its scope
items.note: A workshop goal: which agents are likely going off-rail. Hard because the rails are usually implicit. Much easier under Spacedock, where the entity and stage state the intended scope, which is an argument for F1 rather than for building scope inference from nothing.
items.needs: A declared scope to compare against. Free in Spacedock, guesswork outside it.
items.inferred: Two things, stacked. First the intended scope, which outside Spacedock has no source at all and must be guessed from the opening prompt. Then whether current activity violates it, when touching a neighbouring file, fixing a test or updating an import is routinely legitimate inside any real task.

items.signal: My goals across sessions
items.note: A workshop card, and the same shape as C3: nearly free when a workflow states the goal, hard for an ad-hoc session. It argues for the Spacedock on-ramp rather than for a goal-tracking feature of its own.
items.needs: Spacedock entity state gives this away. Nothing else does.

redundantWith.remains: A read-only roll-up of stated goals for the user's own recall, with no drift decision attached. Its own note admits it is 'the same shape as C3' and argues for the Spacedock on-ramp rather than for a feature. Once C3 compares intent against behaviour, displaying the intent alone is a panel, not a signal.

items.cheaperRoute: Narrower than C3 and scores higher, so it is the version to build.

items.signal: Loop and thrash detector
items.outcome: intervene before the budget is gone
items.note: The narrow, shippable slice of C2: several consecutive failed tool calls, or the same test failing five times in a row. Small enough to build inside one release, and it catches the most expensive failure mode there is, which is burning a whole 5h window on a loop. If C2 feels too big to commit to, commit to this instead.
items.needs: Pattern matching over transcripts Compass already reads.

redundantWith.remains: Nothing additive. C2's own needs list names 'a test re-run loop' and 'repeated identical tool calls' as its detection signals, which is C5's entire definition, so C5's finding set is a proper subset of C2's. Its independent worth is substitution, not addition: build 40 instead of 60, shippable inside one release, and it catches the single most expensive failure mode (a 5h window burned on a loop). Treat these as one line item at two ambition levels and pick one; building C5 then C2 pays the detection cost twice, and scoring both books 172 impact for one capability.

items.cheaperRoute: Narrower than C2 and scores higher, so it is the version to build.

items.signal: Report the irreversible things that happened
items.outcome: find out before the next one
items.note: Rewritten after review. I first wrote this as catching a force push or a dropped table before it lands, which Compass cannot architecturally do: it polls every five seconds, so by the time the tool call shows up in a transcript the command has already run. Stopping something needs DEC-2's write path and a place in the execution path, which is a harness's job rather than a dashboard's. What is left is still worth having, a log of destructive actions across all sessions, and at least it is honest about what it is. The value concentrates in auto-approved sessions, which is exactly where the user turned the harness's own prompts off.
items.needs: Tool-call inspection. It overlaps harness guardrails, so keep the scope narrow.
items.inferred: Which tool calls were irreversible. Literal command shapes (`git push --force`, `DROP TABLE`) are read, not inferred, and that is the honest core. The inference is the boundary: `rm -rf` in a scratch dir, a reset --hard on a branch nobody wanted, a shell one-liner that is arbitrarily destructive.

items.signal: Plan against work actually done
items.note: Kept, but with a conflict I missed the first time. Comparing tracked tasks against the real diff needs semantic judgement, which means a model, and Compass's stated property is that nothing is summarized by a model and no session text leaves the machine. So it needs either a local model or an amendment to a third promise, on top of DEC-1 and DEC-2. That cost was invisible in my first pass, and it is why the score drops rather than any change of view about the idea itself.
items.needs: A local model, or a third amendment. Neither is cheap.
items.inferred: Semantic equivalence between tracked task rows and the actual diff. Requires judging whether a differently-worded implementation satisfies a task, which is model work, and the no-model-summarization promise means it has to be a local model with correspondingly weak judgement.

redundantWith.remains: Drift that stays inside the declared scope: the plan named three tasks, the diff did one, and nothing ever left the rails. C3 cannot see that. The residue is real and expensive, needing semantic judgement, so a local model or a third promise amendment on top of DEC-1 and DEC-2.

items.signal: Two agents in the same repo
items.note: Still the cheapest useful thing here, but less differentiated than I claimed. A careful user does know which sessions are in which directory, which is why the score is 55 rather than the low teens I would have given it under the old axis. The failure is attention rather than access. It stays worth building because the build cost is near zero and the collision is expensive, not because it is a moat.
items.needs: Nothing. The data is on screen already, it is simply never compared.

items.signal: Every session across every harness, one screen
items.note: The one placement still in dispute, and the most consequential one. The board put the cross-harness overview near the easy end. I score it 65, because the definition says quick access and checking tabs across nine harnesses is not quick. The board's entire status-quo row is the user doing this by hand: click into each chat or tab, jump between sessions, stay in the CLI to keep watching. If that is easy, Compass's core is convenience and the differentiated work all sits in the C, D and F items instead. If it is hard, this is the product's floor and it is already built. Worth settling before the roadmap, because it decides whether the shipped product is a wrapper or a foundation.
items.needs: Done.

items.signal: One line saying what this session is
items.needs: Done.
items.subsetNote: D2 subset of D1 - a per-row field of the one-screen view rather than a separate signal.

items.signal: ETA and progress for the current turn
items.note: Shipped, naive by design, and it lands in the differentiated corner at access 78. No harness tells you how long the current turn will take, and the board records the consequence: not knowing how long an agent will take, so you keep coming back. Useful evidence that Compass has already built differentiated things rather than only aggregating.
items.needs: Done.
items.inferred: Remaining time for a turn whose remaining work is unknown. There is no progress denominator: the agent does not know how many tool calls are left, so the ETA is elapsed-time extrapolation over a heavy-tailed distribution where most turns are short and a few are twenty times longer. Shipped and labelled naive, so this risk is realized rather than hypothetical.

items.signal: Notify me when the state changes
items.note: Shipped for needs-input. Native popups on macOS, browser notifications elsewhere, which still need an open tab. Native Linux and Windows backends are the known gap, and H2 is the bigger one.
items.needs: Mostly done. Idle nudges still do not pop on Linux or Windows.

items.signal: Nothing needs you for the next N minutes
items.note: The missing positive signal. Compass says what is happening and what needs you, and never says that you are free, so people keep checking anyway, which is the behaviour the product exists to stop. Moved from Release 1 to Release 2 after review, because I had written that this is only honest once C2 exists and then scheduled it a release earlier anyway. An all-clear that cannot tell a stuck agent from a working one is exactly the promise that loses a user's trust the first time it is wrong.
items.needs: Composable from data already on screen, but it depends on C2 to be truthful.
items.inferred: That nothing needs you for N minutes. Three low-confidence inputs ANDed into one positive assurance: nothing is currently blocked (B1/B2, heuristic on eight of nine harnesses), nothing will block within N minutes (D3's ETAs), and nothing is silently wedged (C2). The all-clear is the product; the components are the weakest signals on the board.

redundantWith.remains: A positive commitment window you can act on where a push cannot reach you: D9 quiet hours, a muted phone, a meeting, or the Linux/Windows machines D4's own note admits have no native popup backend. It is also the only signal that survives a delivery failure, because silence from D4 is indistinguishable from 'nothing happened' and 'the notifier is broken', whereas an explicit 'clear for 40 minutes' is falsifiable. That is failure-mode insurance, not a second copy of the walk-away promise.

items.signal: Come back at 3:40
items.note: The board sticky about ETAs taken to its conclusion: not twelve of them, one clock time, the soonest moment anything will want you. Unlike D5 this stays honest without C2, because it only claims when something is expected to finish and never that all is well. That is why it can carry Release 1 on its own.
items.needs: The minimum over ETAs Compass already computes.
items.inferred: The minimum over D3's per-turn ETAs, presented as one clock time. The claim is genuinely weaker than D5's, but the behaviour it induces is not: hand someone a single time to come back and they will leave the desk, so in practice it functions as an all-clear it never states. That gap is where the risk was banked as differentiation.

redundantWith.remains: One clock time you can write on a calendar or hand to someone else, which supports pre-committing to a 20-minute errand before leaving rather than reacting after a ping. It also stays honest without C2 while D5 does not, so it can carry Release 1 alone. Both of those are sequencing and packaging value; once H2 delivers D4 off the desk, nobody needs to remember 3:40 because 3:40 will call them.

items.cheaperRoute: Narrower than D3 and scores higher, so it is the version to build.

items.signal: Ordered by what needs you most
items.outcome: stop triaging by whatever you saw first
items.note: The board names the failure plainly: I deal with the thing that I see, without priority. Calm mode's attention sort is most of the answer already. It is not the default, and the card view does not have it at all.
items.needs: Make it the default, and bring it to both display modes.
items.scoreBasis: panel median of 3 blind lenses; re-read as an action, not information

items.signal: Stake of the task
items.note: The board already placed this at low impact, and I agree, for a reason worth saying out loud. Nobody will maintain a stakes field by hand. It only works if it is inferred from something like a production versus scratch repo, a branch name, or the presence of a deploy step. Inferred stakes that are wrong are worse than no stakes at all, because people act on them.
items.needs: Either a declaration nobody keeps up to date, or inference that has to be right.
items.inferred: Stake, from proxies nobody validated: a repo name, a branch name, the presence of a deploy step. Each proxy fails routinely. `main` in a scratch repo, a feature branch that deploys to prod, a repo called sandbox that holds the production config.

items.signal: Quiet hours
items.outcome: protect a block of deep work
items.note: Suppress everything except your-call. Small and obvious, and the kind of absence that gets a tool uninstalled in week two.
items.needs: A settings surface, which the board already asks for.

items.signal: A digest of what happened while you were away
items.note: Three finished, one needs you, one stuck. Coming back is a different moment from watching, and today it costs a full re-scan of the board.
items.needs: H1. Compass keeps no history at all right now.
items.inferred: Every bucket in 'three finished, one needs you, one stuck' is a separate detector: E2's completion inference, B1/B2's needs-input, C2's wedge verdict. The digest also implies completeness, and a re-entry summary that omits a session reads as an all-clear about that session.
items.subsetNote: D10 subset of (D7 + E2 + E3 + C2) - 'three finished, one needs you, one stuck' is the live board grouped and sorted; only transitions that resolved while away are outside that union.

redundantWith.remains: Only the transitions that resolved while you were gone and no longer appear in current state: a session that blocked and was auto-continued, a task that failed then passed, an error that scrolled away. Everything else in its own example ('three finished, one needs you, one stuck') is D7 ordering over E2, C2 and B1 flags, computable from the live board with no H1 at all. So D10's honest scope is a change log, not a digest, and it is the only part of it that justifies the history store.

items.signal: Reach the user away from the desk
items.note: A hole I missed completely on the first pass. Half this board argues that the product's job is to let you stop watching, and every delivery path it has requires you to be at the machine: a macOS popup, or a browser notification that needs an open tab. The moment a user takes the advice and leaves, every signal stops reaching them. D4, D5 and D6 all quietly assume someone sitting in front of the laptop.
items.needs: Some path off the machine, which reopens the local-only question from a different direction than DEC-1 does.

items.signal: Stale, meaning idle two hours or more
items.outcome: notice the ones that went quiet
items.note: Shipped as a calm-mode flag, with an honest gloss in the docs: either it finished and nobody read it, or it is waiting on a reply that never came.
items.needs: Done.
items.subsetNote: E1 subset of (E2 union E3) - E1's documented gloss is E2 and E3 unseparated, and E2's note says separating them is the entire value.

redundantWith.remains: The honest catch-all for harnesses where neither a SessionEnd nor a completion classifier fires, which E3's own note says is most of the other eight. As a user-facing signal it is fully subsumed: its documented gloss ('either it finished and nobody read it, or it is waiting on a reply that never came') is a confession that it is E2 and E3 unseparated, and E2's note says splitting them is the entire value. Being shipped is why the penalty is a scoring correction rather than a build decision.

items.signal: Finished, and nobody read it
items.outcome: collect work you already paid for
items.note: The board's line about seeing things done and closing the tab. E1 lumps this together with abandoned sessions, and splitting the two is the entire value, because one is a reward and the other is a chore.
items.needs: Tell idle-after-completion apart from idle-after-question. Both signals already exist.

redundantWith.remains: Almost all of it. Finished-and-unread is a reward you collect and died-rather-than-finished is a chore you restart; the remedies are opposite, so these are siblings rather than duplicates. Listed to record that the overlap was checked: they share only the detector that decides why a session went quiet, so build one classifier with two outputs and count the value once.

items.signal: Died, rather than finished
items.note: A crashed session reads as Idle today, which looks identical to done, so the user waits on something that is never coming back. Cheap for harnesses that write a SessionEnd, inference everywhere else.
items.needs: SessionEnd already arrives for Claude. The other eight vary.

items.signal: Ended with uncommitted work
items.note: This is how agent work actually gets lost. Not dramatically, but in a dirty worktree nobody went back to. Compass already knows every session's working directory, which is the hard half of the problem.
items.needs: Bigger than I first called it. I described this as a smaller policy question than DEC-1, and that was wrong. SECURITY.md treats file reads outside the documented store paths as a security bug, with one narrow and heavily guarded exception for Spacedock frontmatter. Reading git state inside a user's repository is a third amendment, and arguably more invasive than fetching a quota number, because it touches their code rather than their account.
items.scoreBasis: panel median of 3 blind lenses; boundary audit, promote, strong
items.cheaperRoute: Narrower than E5 and scores higher, so it is the version to build.

items.signal: Branch or PR left behind
items.needs: Everything E4 needs, plus a remote call for PR state.

redundantWith.remains: The review-stalled case a dirty-tree check cannot see: work committed and pushed, tree clean, branch or PR sitting untouched. That is a different loss (stalled in review) from E4's (never saved), and it needs a remote call E4 does not. It also needs everything E4 needs first, per its own note, so it can never ship earlier or cheaper.

items.signal: Mark it handled and clear it
items.note: The board asks twice for a list of only active things, with closed ones hidden. It needs somewhere to remember dismissals, which would be the first piece of user state Compass owns.
items.needs: A small local state file. Compass already writes under ~/.compass.

items.signal: Hand-off prompt when the wall is coming
items.outcome: the next session picks up cleanly
items.note: My favourite item, because the user already invented it. The board records the manual ritual word for word: if the limit is approaching I will pause the job, ask for a summary of what has been done, and get a prompt I can give a follow-up session. That is a workaround with a shape, and automating a ritual somebody already performs by hand is the highest-confidence bet available, because the demand is demonstrated rather than guessed at.
items.needs: A1 to know the wall is coming, and a way to ask the session for a summary, which is a narrower slice of DEC-2 than B4 wants.
items.inferred: That the wall is coming, at full inheritance from A5's projection, plus the choice of the moment to fire. The hand-off text itself is the agent's own work, not Compass's inference, which is what keeps this below A5.

redundantWith.remains: Continuity of context, which no hatch provides. A3 and A4 keep a machine working; E7 keeps the work coherent across the break. It also automates a ritual the board records the user already performing by hand, which is the highest-confidence demand signal here. Genuinely distinct value, listed only to show the escape-hatch overlap was checked and does not apply.

items.scoreBasis: panel median of 3 blind lenses; re-read as an action, not information

items.signal: These four are one project, make it a workflow
items.note: On the board already: group them if they are on the same project, and treat that as a potential workflow. This is the Spacedock on-ramp, and the only item where Compass's read-only vantage point is an advantage rather than a limit, because it can see the pattern precisely by watching everything and owning nothing. Note the score split: spotting the group is trivial information, and proposing a workflow worth accepting is the whole build.
items.needs: Grouping by project and overlapping time is easy. Proposing a good workflow is not.

redundantWith.remains: The unprompted noticing: you cannot promote a project you had not realised was one project, and F1 is the only item that spots the group. Shipped alone, though, it is a suggestion with no accept button, which is a nag rather than a capability, and F6 requires it anyway. Its real independent worth is being the cheap probe of whether users want the promotion at all before DEC-2 is paid for.

items.cheaperRoute: Narrower than F6 and scores higher, so it is the version to build.

items.signal: You have done this five times, make it a skill
items.note: Board sticky, and the flywheel into Spacedock cloud. The second half is stronger than the first: agents keep asking you the same question, so take yourself out of that decision. It reframes a repeated interruption as a defect in the setup rather than a cost of doing business.
items.needs: H1, the same history store D10 and F3 need.
items.inferred: That N past interactions were 'the same thing'. That is semantic clustering of prompts and decisions, which needs judgement the no-model promise forbids, on top of a history store (H1) that does not exist yet.

redundantWith.remains: A different granularity of the same move: automate a repeated decision rather than a repeated project, so the target is a skill and not a workflow. That distinction survives F6 intact. What does not survive is the framing value, since once F6 has changed the user's role from operator to orchestrator, F2 is an optimisation inside the new role rather than the thing that changes it.

items.signal: Where your attention actually went
items.note: Hours spent answering agents, and which decisions keep repeating. Nobody delegates because they were told to; they delegate when shown their own week. This is the evidence layer under F1 and F2, and the one artifact here a user would voluntarily show their manager. It differs from G4 in that it exists to change behaviour rather than to be admired.
items.needs: H1. Nothing leaves the machine.
items.inferred: Hours of human attention. Compass can see when a gate opened and when it closed, but not whether the user was attending in between, so wall-clock gaps include lunch and sleep. The headline number is systematically inflated, or if measured from activity, systematically deflated.

redundantWith.remains: The artifact for a human audience: the week you can show a manager, or yourself, to authorise the delegation. That is persuasion, not capability, and its own note is explicit that it exists to change behaviour. It survives as the reason someone accepts F1's proposal, and it collapses as an independent outcome, because attention data nobody acts on is G4 with better framing.

items.signal: Keep a history of what happened
items.note: Added after review, because four items were quietly resting on a foundation that appeared nowhere on the board. D10, F2, F3 and A6 all need Compass to remember yesterday, and today it remembers nothing between refreshes. Its own impact is modest, since a history nobody queries is worth nothing, but the sequencing matters: it has to land before the release that depends on it, and nothing in the plan currently says so.
items.needs: A local event store, and a retention policy. It also turns Compass into something that accumulates data about the user, which is a smaller version of the same trust question as DEC-1.

items.signal: Cloud and local on one board
items.note: Board sticky. Also the point where local-only stops being available as a promise, which is worth deciding on purpose rather than arriving at by accident.
items.needs: Remote sources, auth, and the end of the local-only story.

items.signal: Cowork and hosted sessions
items.note: Board sticky, filed as a question rather than a feature: check whether Claude Cowork sessions can show in Compass, since ChatGPT has something similar. Answer the feasibility question before ranking it, because the answer is probably binary.
items.needs: It depends entirely on whether a local artifact exists. Currently unknown.

redundantWith.remains: Entirely contingent, and the contingency is worth resolving before scoring it: if Cowork writes a local artifact, F5 is just another collector and owes nothing to F4; if it does not, F5 is F4's remote-source work applied to one more vendor. Its own note files it as a feasibility question, which is the right treatment. Answer that first, then it is either cheap and independent or subsumed.

items.signal: Promote a session to a workflow
items.note: The workshop sticky is the destination: you are the orchestrator, move up to Spacedock and let the FO be the orchestrator. F1 spots the pattern, this acts on it, and it is the moment the user's role changes. Marked down from 94 on the same grounds as B4. It is the strategic reason Compass belongs to Spacedock rather than being a standalone utility, and that is an argument about position, not about how much pain it removes this quarter.
items.needs: DEC-2's write path plus workflow generation. The most expensive item here.
items.inferred: The workflow to generate. Turning an observed session pattern into stages, entities and a first-officer contract worth accepting is a semantic judgement, and it is a write, not a readout.
items.scoreBasis: panel median of 3 blind lenses; boundary audit, demote, strong

items.signal: Across machines, or across a team
items.note: A laptop and a dev box today, a team tomorrow. It changes the product category and the trust model at the same time.
items.needs: Transport, identity, and everything F4 needs.
items.subsetNote: F7 subset of F4 - F7's needs line is 'everything F4 needs' plus machine identity.

redundantWith.remains: Machine identity and other people's sessions, which is a different buyer and arguably a different product; F4 stops at 'my cloud and my laptop'. Everything underneath it, transport, auth and the end of the local-only story, is F4's work, as its own needs line concedes.

items.signal: Token rate sparkline
items.note: Shipped, and pleasant to look at. A rate with no ceiling supports no decision on its own. A1 gives it one, and the same pixels start meaning something, which is an argument for the usage cluster that has nothing to do with quota panic.
items.needs: Done.
items.subsetNote: G1 subset of A5 - the rate without a ceiling versus the rate projected against one; A5 is G1 plus the number that makes it a decision.

items.signal: Count of active sessions
items.note: A number with no verb after it. Fine as furniture, never a reason to open the tab.
items.needs: Done.

items.signal: Which model each session is running
items.outcome: move cheap work off the expensive model
items.note: Raised from 30 after review, and it was probably a miss first time round. Seeing that a session is burning Opus on something trivial is directly actionable on its own, and it is the control surface A3 needs, because knowing the Opus limit is close is useless unless you can see which sessions are spending it.

Mostly survives; the overlap is confined to the one case where the Opus-heavy session is also the top consumer.

items.note: Vanity metrics. Listed so the low-impact quadrant is honestly populated, and so the no is on the record rather than merely implied.
items.needs: H1, which is a poor reason to build H1.

F3's dataset (hours spent answering agents, which decisions repeat) strictly contains G4's (sessions this week, streaks), computed from the same H1 store. Its own note already files it as vanity listed for honesty. If F3 ships, G4 is a stylesheet over data that is already there; if F3 does not, G4 is a poor reason to build H1, which its needs line concedes.

decisions.title: Let Compass read your quota
decisions.framing: The board's highest-value cluster needs quota numbers. Codex writes its own rate-limit snapshots (5-hour and weekly used_percent, resets_at, plan, credits) into session JSONL that Compass already reads; checked on disk 2026-08-04. Claude Code stores nothing quota-shaped locally, and a survey of all nine buckets (in DRC-4053) found every other harness either fetches quota over an authenticated API or has no quota of its own. So the Codex slice ships under the existing promises, and the decision is how Compass gets Claude's numbers, and any other vendor's that live only behind an API.
breaks: A third network behaviour appears. SECURITY.md today describes exactly two components that touch the network, both bound to loopback.

It needs a credential, and that is the real escalation rather than the network call. Compass would read the harness's own OAuth token: a macOS Keychain item that can prompt on first read, or a file under ~/.claude on Linux. A different class of access from reading transcripts.

The quota endpoint is undocumented. Calling it with the harness's token from outside the harness is tolerated today but unsupported, and an expired token forces a choice: show stale data, or attempt a refresh and risk racing the harness for its own session. Never refresh; stale beats a broken login.

The cost repeats per quota authority, not per harness. Goose, OpenCode and Pi borrow their provider's quota, so one Claude fetcher answers for every harness on the same subscription; Gemini, Antigravity, Cursor, Droid and Copilot's allowance each need their own authenticated integration.
survives: Session data never leaves the machine, unchanged. The request carries a credential and returns quota numbers. No transcript content, no prompts, no paths, no project names.
The server still binds 127.0.0.1 and nothing else. That invariant is about the listening socket, and an outbound read does not touch it.

options.name: Read the quota harnesses already write to disk (do first; needs no decision)
options.pro: Codex publishes rate-limit snapshots into session files Compass already parses. Both invariants intact, no credential, nothing to install, a small parsing job, and it settles the display questions (staleness, as-of timestamps) before any credential is touched.
options.con: Covers exactly one harness: the survey found nobody else writing quota to disk. The snapshot is only as fresh as the last active turn, so the tile must carry an as-of timestamp.

options.name: The server fetches it, behind a configurable opt-out flag
options.pro: RECOMMENDED (owner's lean, 2026-08-04). Highest fidelity, works for every user out of the box, one code path. A user who installs a visibility dashboard has already decided they want to see what their harnesses are doing, and quota is part of that. The trust story survives: what users rely on is that session data stays on the machine and Compass sends nothing it gathers to any other service, and a quota request that carries a credential out and brings numbers back moves none of it.
options.con: The server gains credential access and its first outbound call, so SECURITY.md's scope must be rewritten before the code lands, and default-on means the amendment applies to everyone rather than only to users who asked.

options.name: Read a cache another tool already maintains
options.pro: The no-network promise stays literally true, and Barista already writes the 5-hour and weekly figures.
options.con: Not a third architecture: it is C with a sidecar we neither version nor control, and Barista's cache lacks A3's per-model sub-limits. Keep it only as an opportunistic read, never a required dependency.

options.name: An opt-in sidecar writes a local cache the server reads
options.pro: It matches an architecture Compass already has. notify_hook.py is exactly this shape: a small, separately invoked, user-installed component with its own narrow network contract. The dashboard server keeps both invariants and reads one more local file, which is what it already does for nine harnesses.
options.con: Two things to install and an empty tile until opt-in; every credential hazard from A moves into the sidecar rather than disappearing; and nothing naturally triggers polling quota, so it needs an invocation design and a staleness contract.

decisions.ask: Two calls, not one. First, D was never gated: ship the Codex tile. Second, pick the fetch's home for Claude's numbers: in the server behind a configurable opt-out (A, the owner's lean) or in an opt-in sidecar (C). Whichever ships: the request carries the credential and nothing else, the token is never refreshed, and the SECURITY.md scope lands in the same PR as the code.

decisions.title: Let Compass act, not just observe
decisions.framing: The second invariant is read-only access to harness stores. Answering a prompt from the dashboard, asking a session for a hand-off summary, and promoting a session to a workflow all need a write path into a running harness.
breaks: Invariant 2, directly, with no narrow reading available. There is no version of this where the write is not a write.
A loopback server that can act on your behalf is a materially different thing to leave running detached. The threat model needs rewriting rather than amending.
No harness offers a supported way in, so it means terminal injection or private per-harness channels, across nine harnesses and three platforms.

It fights the positioning. Compass sells itself as harness-agnostic, and a write path has to be built and maintained nine times. The same is true of DEC-1's per-vendor quota work. Both decisions quietly trade agnosticism for depth, and that trade is worth naming now rather than discovering later.
survives: Not much. This is a genuine category change: Compass stops being a map and becomes a console.

options.name: Not yet, ship the cheap half
options.pro: RECOMMENDED FOR NOW. B5 captures much of the value by ending the hunt across tabs without any write path. Ship it and find out whether the remaining friction is the trip or the answering, because right now that is an assumption rather than a finding.
options.con: Leaves the highest-ceiling item on the board unbuilt.

options.name: A write path scoped to Spacedock only
options.pro: Spacedock has its own state files and conventions, so a gate can be answered by writing state rather than injecting into a terminal. Narrow, supported, and where F6 wants to end up anyway.
options.con: It only helps Spacedock users, which cuts against the board's own line that users are not required to use Spacedock.

options.name: A general write path across harnesses
options.pro: The full prize, B4 and F6 both.
options.con: Fragile everywhere, and it ends the read-only story for every user including the ones who only ever wanted a dashboard.

decisions.ask: Worth settling the direction now even if none of it gets built this quarter, because B5, E7 and F6 all sequence differently depending on the answer.
